parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
One mole of a monatomic ideal gas starts at 80°C in a thermally insulated cylinder. Compression does 50 J of work on the gas. What is its final temperature?

A. 480°C
B. 400°C
C. 84°C
D. 4°C

answer.text: C. Insulation gives Q=0, so ΔU=+50 J. For one mole of monatomic ideal gas, ΔU=(3/2)RΔT, giving ΔT=4.0 K. The final temperature is 84°C.

parts.display_text:
An ideal monatomic gas is kept at constant temperature. A graph of its pressure p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin with gradient q. Using pV=nRT, what is the gas’s internal energy?

A. 2q/3
B. 2/(3q)
C. 3q/2
D. 3/(2q)

answer.text: C. The line is p=q/V, so pV=q=nRT. A monatomic ideal gas has U=(3/2)nRT=3q/2.

A monatomic ideal gas completes a cycle consisting of isothermal compression, adiabatic expansion and heating at constant volume. Which pressure–volume diagram represents this cycle?

A. Diagram A
B. Diagram B
C. Diagram C
D. Diagram D

answer.text: B. Compression follows an isotherm toward smaller volume. Adiabatic expansion returns along the lower, steeper curve, after which heating raises pressure vertically at constant volume. These arrows and shapes occur in B.

parts.display_text: A sample containing 18.66 mol of monatomic ideal gas starts at 293 K. It receives 13.2 kJ of heat at constant volume, then expands adiabatically to twice that volume. Use R=8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate (a) the temperature increase during heating and (b) the final temperature after expansion.

answer.text: (a) W=0 at constant volume, so Q=ΔU=³⁄₂nRΔT. Thus ΔT≈56.7 K and the heated gas reaches about 349.7 K. (b) For a monatomic ideal gas, TV²⁄³ is constant in the adiabatic model. Tfinal=349.7/2²⁄³≈220 K.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: In an isolated ice–water system, 50 g of water freezes at 273.15 K and releases 16.7 kJ. That energy warms initially colder ice from 241.15 K to 273.15 K. (a) Estimate the entropy change of the freezing water. (b) Explain whether the total entropy of the isolated system increases, decreases or remains constant.

answer.text: (a) The water loses heat at constant temperature: ΔS=Q/T=−16700/273.15≈−61.1 J K⁻¹. (b) Total entropy increases. The colder ice gains the transferred energy at lower temperatures and therefore gains more entropy than the freezing water loses. This spontaneous heat transfer is irreversible.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Equal samples of the same ideal gas undergo the same temperature increase. One expands at constant pressure; the other is heated in a rigid container. Use the first law to explain which requires less energy by heating.

answer.text: Both have the same increase in internal energy because the gas and temperature rise are the same. The rigid container has ΔV = 0, hence W = 0. The expanding gas also does positive work. Since Q = ΔU + W, the rigid-container sample requires less energy by heating.

parts.display_text: An ideal gas is heated in a sealed rigid chamber. Sketch its path on a pressure–volume diagram and on an internal-energy–volume diagram, with arrows. Explain the shapes.

answer.text: Both paths are vertical upward lines at the same positive, constant volume. Heating increases temperature, so pressure and internal energy increase. Because ΔV = 0, boundary work is zero and the energy supplied increases internal energy.

parts.display_text: The first law is written Q = ΔU + W. State the meaning and positive sign convention of each term.

answer.text: Q is energy transferred to the system by heating; it is positive for heat input. ΔU is the increase in the system’s internal energy. W is work done by the system on its surroundings; it is positive for expansion work.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: An insulated room contains an empty refrigerator with its door open. The refrigerator is powered by electricity from outside the room. Taking the entire room and refrigerator as the system, use the first law to decide whether its internal energy increases, decreases or stays constant.

answer.text: The internal energy increases. No heat crosses the insulated boundary, so Q = 0. Electrical work is done on the system, meaning Wby < 0. Thus ΔU = Q − Wby > 0. Transfers between the open refrigerator and the room do not remove energy from the whole system.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A cyclic heat engine takes energy QH from a hot reservoir at TH and produces work. Explain what other energy transfer is required and why its maximum theoretical efficiency is less than 100% for a cold reservoir at TC > 0 K.

answer.text: Some energy QC must be rejected to the cold reservoir. The maximum efficiency is ηmax = 1 − TC/TH, so it is below 1 when TC > 0 K. A cyclic engine cannot convert all heat drawn from one reservoir into work.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A fixed amount of ideal gas follows cycle A → B → C → D → A in the pressure–volume graph. The second graph gives its internal energy. X has units of volume and Y has units of pressure.

(a) State the first law using Q for energy supplied by heating and W_by for work done by the gas.
(b) Use the graphs to find U in terms of p and V. Then use pV = Nk_BT to express U in terms of N and T, defining k_B.
(c) Find the work done ON the gas during A → B and C → D.
(d) Find the net heat supplied over a complete cycle and explain your reasoning.

answer.text:
(a) Q = ΔU + W_by, where heat into the gas and work done by it are positive.
(b) At A, pV = 12XY and U = 18XY; the other labelled states give the same ratio. Thus U = 3pV/2 = 3Nk_BT/2, with k_B the Boltzmann constant.
(c) A → B is compression at 2Y: W_on = −pΔV = +8XY. C → D is expansion at 5Y: W_on = −20XY.
(d) The vertical paths do no work. The gas returns to its initial state, so ΔU_cycle = 0. Net work by the gas is 20XY − 8XY = 12XY, hence net heat supplied Q = +12XY.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A fixed amount of monatomic ideal gas is held at constant pressure 1.6 × 10⁵ Pa. The graph shows its volume against Celsius temperature. Determine the work done ON the gas as its temperature rises from 0 °C to 210 °C.

answer.text: The graph gives V_initial ≈ 0.18 m³ and V_final ≈ 0.32 m³. Work by the gas is pΔV = (1.6 × 10⁵)(0.32 − 0.18) = +2.24 × 10⁴ J. Work on the gas is the negative of this, about −2.2 × 10⁴ J.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: The source pressure-volume diagram shows paths A and B taking an ideal gas from state 1 to state 3, while path C returns isothermally. Use the graph to find ΔU, work done on the gas and heating for A+B, then compare the magnitude and sign of work done on the gas during C.

answer.text: States 1 and 3 have the same temperature, so ΔU=0. Along A+B the gas expands at 100 kPa from 1×10⁻³ to 4×10⁻³ m³: work done by the gas is +300 J (work on it −300 J), hence Q=+300 J. In C the gas is compressed, so work done on it is positive and its magnitude is smaller because the area under C is smaller.

fep-d5113d0c3f9c0cb5-q16:whole.hint: Work is connected to the change in volume. On a pressure–volume graph, look for the relevant area.
notes: Work done by a gas is W = ∫p dV; at constant pressure it becomes pΔV. Expansion gives positive work by the gas, compression negative.
The enclosed area of a complete cycle is net work, with its sign set by the direction around the cycle. Convert kPa, MPa, litres and any axis multipliers before calculating.

fep-d5113d0c3f9c0cb5-q18:whole.hint: Draw the energy entering from the hot reservoir, the useful work and the energy rejected to the cold reservoir.
notes: Over a complete engine cycle ΔU = 0, so W = Q_hot − Q_cold and efficiency = W/Q_hot. Use energy per cycle or power consistently.
Only an ideal reversible Carnot engine reaches η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot. Both reservoir temperatures must be in kelvin; this gives an upper bound for a real engine.

original-ib26mb1a-mcq-15:whole.hint: Apply the first law using the fact that work is done on the gas, then convert the internal-energy change into a temperature rise.
notes: With W defined as work done by the gas, compression has W=−50 J and ΔU=Q−W=+50 J.
A temperature change has the same numerical value in kelvin and Celsius. Add that change to the initial temperature; do not report the rise as the final temperature.

original-ib26mc1a-mcq-13:whole.hint: Express the equation of the straight line using its stated axes, then relate the gradient to internal energy.
notes: The gradient has units Pa divided by m⁻³, giving Pa m³=J; an energy should be proportional to q rather than 1/q.
The factor 3/2 applies to the internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas. The ideal-gas state relation is supplied.

original-ib26mc1a-mcq-14:whole.hint: Check each process direction as well as the curve shape; constant-volume heating must be a vertical upward segment.
notes: From a common state, adiabatic expansion cools the gas and decreases pressure faster than isothermal expansion.
A pressure–volume curve for isothermal expansion slopes downward. Diagrams with both curves rising with volume cannot describe the stated cycle.

original-ib26mb2-written-2-c-d:whole.hint: Treat the two processes separately. The second process begins at the temperature reached after the first.
notes: Use the monatomic internal-energy expression only because the gas is explicitly monatomic. Constant volume makes the first-stage work zero.
Adiabatic means no heat transfer; it does not mean constant temperature. Expansion does work at the expense of internal energy, so the gas cools.

original-ib26mc2-written-3-bii-biii:whol.hint: Keep the sign of heat transfer for the water. Then distinguish its entropy change from that of the entire isolated system.
notes: The second law applies to total entropy of an isolated system; an individual part may lose entropy while the rest gains more.
Do not apply Q/T using a single arbitrary temperature to the ice while its temperature changes. The qualitative comparison follows because its heat is received below the water’s freezing temperature.

cross-ca24m4-written-2c:whole.hint: Compare the work done in the two processes before comparing Q.
notes: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends on temperature. Equal temperature rises do not imply equal heat input when the amounts of work differ.

cross-ap24p2-written-2b:whole.hint: What does a rigid chamber imply about the horizontal coordinate on both graphs?
notes: An isochoric process has no area under its p–V path and hence no boundary work. The path is at the actual nonzero chamber volume, not on the vertical axis.

cross-aq24eng-written-4.1:whole.hint: Each sign depends on whether energy enters or leaves the chosen system.
notes: Keep one convention throughout: IB uses positive W for work done by the gas. If a source instead defines work done on the gas, its first-law equation has a different sign.

cross-aq24eng-written-4.2:whole.hint: Draw the system boundary around both the room and the refrigerator.
notes: Insulated does not mean isolated from work. Electrical input crosses the boundary even though heat transfer through the walls is zero.

cross-aq24eng-written-4.3-4.4:whole.hint: The first law alone is not enough: consider the second law and both reservoirs.
notes: Use absolute temperatures in the Carnot efficiency. A hypothetical 100% value would require a zero-kelvin cold reservoir in this model.

cross-ca25n42-written-4-a-bi-bii-ci-cii-.hint: Read the coordinates of every corner carefully. Keep separate columns for work done by the gas and work done on it.
notes: The IB convention Q = ΔU + W uses work done by the gas. If a question asks for work on the gas, reverse that work sign, not the heat sign.
A full cycle restores internal energy but need not give zero heat or work. The enclosed pressure–volume area gives the net work; clockwise circulation here makes work by the gas positive.
Read C and D at 5Y: 4Y is an axis tick, not the upper path. XY has energy units because Pa m³ = J.

cross-ca25m42-written-3-bi:whole.hint: Read both volumes, then decide the work sign from whether the gas expands or is compressed.
notes: The IB convention takes work done by the system as positive. The question asks for work on the gas, so the sign reverses. Area under a volume–temperature graph is not work.

cross-fast-ap-70b65f74d52fb39a-1-ab1:who.hint: Use ideal-gas temperature proportional to PV, and read work from signed area under the pressure-volume path.
notes: The IB guide uses Clausius convention: Q supplied and work done by the gas are positive.
Thermodynamic cycles and the first law in this form are additional higher level B.4 content.

fep-314acbf92ebc17fd-qE2:a.iii.text: Use the boiler as the hot reservoir and the condenser as the cold reservoir. The maximum thermal efficiency is ηmax = 1 − Tcondenser/Tboiler, with both temperatures expressed in kelvin.

fep-314acbf92ebc17fd-qE2:b.i.text: The high-temperature energy supplied at the boiler is higher-quality energy. The thermal energy rejected at the colder condenser is lower-quality energy because a smaller fraction can be converted into useful work.

fep-314acbf92ebc17fd-qE2:b.ii.text: Energy is conserved, but some is transferred to the cold reservoir as thermal energy. This dispersed, lower-temperature energy is less available for conversion to useful work, so its quality has decreased.

fep-314acbf92ebc17fd-qE2:c.text: An irreversible process increases total entropy as energy becomes more dispersed. More of the conserved energy is then unavailable for useful work. Increased entropy describes this loss of energy quality, not destruction of energy.

fep-aae5041a67de03ff-qB4:1.i.text: For one isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, ΔU = 0 and all the heat supplied becomes work. This is not a complete repeating cycle: the gas has expanded. Returning it to its initial state requires compression and, in an engine cycle, heat rejection. A cyclic engine cannot turn all of its heat input into net work without rejecting heat.
